chapter_summary:
Understanding the operational status of your Juniper device is the first and most crucial step in network management and troubleshooting. Junos OS provides a rich set of `show` commands, executed from the operational mode, that allow you to inspect nearly every aspect of the device's current state. These commands are non-disruptive; they simply display information without making any changes to the configuration. Familiarity with these commands forms the bedrock of effective monitoring.

One of the most frequently used commands is `show interfaces`. This command provides a comprehensive overview of all network interfaces on the device. When you execute `show interfaces`, you'll see details like the physical link status (up/down), administrative status (enabled/disabled), input and output traffic statistics (bytes, packets), and error counters. For example, if an interface shows "Link-level type: Ethernet, MTU: 1514, Speed: 1000mbps, Duplex: Full, Role: None, State: Up, Physical link is Up", you know the physical connection is healthy. However, if you see high "Input errors" or "Output errors", it might indicate a duplex mismatch, a faulty cable, or a problem with the connected device. It's common for new administrators to overlook these error counters, but they are vital clues for diagnosing intermittent connectivity issues or degraded performance. Always examine the `Errors` and `Drops` sections for any non-zero or increasing values, as these often point to underlying physical or data link layer problems.

Verifying connectivity and reachability across your network often involves inspecting the routing table. The `show route` command is indispensable for this purpose. It displays all the routes that the Junos device has learned, either directly connected, statically configured, or dynamically learned via routing protocols like OSPF or BGP. When you execute `show route`, you'll see the destination network, the protocol from which the route was learned, its preference (administrative distance), metric, and the next-hop address. For instance, `show route 192.168.1.0/24` will show you how to reach that specific subnet. If a route is missing, or points to an incorrect next-hop, it directly impacts network reachability. A common mistake is assuming a route exists just because a routing protocol is configured; always verify its presence and correctness in the routing table. You can also use `show route protocol ospf` or `show route table inet.0` to filter the output and focus on specific routing protocols or routing instances. The `inet.0` table is the default IPv4 unicast routing table.

Beyond interfaces and routing, it's critical to monitor the overall health of the Junos device itself. Commands like `show system processes extensive` can reveal CPU utilization for various processes, helping identify if a particular process is hogging resources. `show system memory` provides insights into memory usage, indicating if the device is running low on available RAM, which could lead to performance degradation or instability. Similarly, `show system storage` displays disk space utilization, which is important for ensuring enough space for logs, configuration backups, and future software upgrades. A full disk can prevent new logs from being written or even prevent the device from booting correctly. Regularly checking these system health metrics can help you proactively identify potential issues before they escalate into service outages. Remember, these `show` commands are executed from the operational mode, which is the default mode after logging in or exiting configuration mode using the `exit` command. To enter configuration mode, you type `configure`. To return to operational mode, you type `exit` or `quit`.

screens.title: Monitoring Junos OS Operational Status
screens.subtitle: Using operational-mode show commands to observe interfaces, routes, and system health

narration.text: Monitoring a Junos device begins with learning how to read its operational outputs. In this lesson you'll learn a small set of non-disruptive show commands that reveal interface state, traffic counters, error rates, routing decisions, and system health. Practically, this means you can verify whether a link is physically up, whether an expected route exists and which next hop it uses, and whether C P U, memory, or disk usage needs attention. For example, you will use show interfaces terse to find an interface, then show interfaces extensive to inspect bytes, drops, and CRC counters. You will also use show route and targeted variants like show route 0.0.0.0/0 to confirm a default route and its next hop. Finally, system checks such as show system processes and show system storage help prevent surprises like a full disk or runaway process. Throughout, watch for common misconceptions: a configured routing protocol does not guarantee a learned route, and a link that reports up may still have CRC errors. As you proceed, think how these quick, read-only checks let you form a hypothesis before changing configuration or replacing hardware.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Show commands give a live snapshot of device state. They are safe, non-disruptive, and essential for fast troubleshooting and verification.

screens.title: Operational Mode and Show Commands
screens.subtitle: What operational mode means and why show commands are safe

narration.text: Operational mode in Junos is the read-only workspace you land in after logging in. It gives you immediate access to a suite of show commands that display the device's current state without modifying configuration. This distinction matters: configuration mode is for making persistent changes, whereas operational commands are safe to run in production because they only report information. In practice you'll use operational mode every time you need to verify an interface state, check routing, or inspect resource usage before acting. A concrete example is running show interfaces terse to confirm that an interface is up and has an IP. A common misconception is to confuse configured state with operational state — an interface may be configured as enabled but still be down due to a physical link problem. Operational commands reveal the real-time status. Another subtle point: some show outputs can be filtered or paged; using pipe modifiers and no-more helps when you want unbroken output. The core insight is this: always gather operational evidence first. That evidence frames whether you should change configuration, replace hardware, or escalate to the application owner.

keyIdea.title: Operational vs Configuration
keyIdea.text: Operational mode is for observation and diagnostics; configuration mode is for making changes.

content.html:
Definition

Operational mode

Operational mode provides non-disruptive commands to inspect live device state such as interfaces, routes, and system health.

Why this is safe
  • Show commands only display state; they do not commit configuration changes.
  • Use these commands to form a hypothesis before changing config or replacing hardware.
  • Pipe modifiers like | no-more prevent paging during long outputs.
Key Takeaway

Start every troubleshooting exercise by collecting operational-mode evidence; it reduces guesswork and helps target the fix.

Concrete examples
Example: Verify you are in operational mode
user@device> show system uptime
user@device> show interfaces terse
Misconception
Configured 'enabled' does not guarantee 'up'. Operational outputs show the real-time link and counters that prove health.
Check your understanding
If an interface is configured but traffic fails, what would you check first with show commands? (Hint: link state and error counters.)

screens.title: show interfaces terse — find an interface quickly
screens.subtitle: Using terse output to identify interfaces and addresses

narration.text: Show interfaces terse is your first fast check. It lists all interfaces with administrative and link states and the protocols and addresses bound to logical units. Use it to quickly identify which physical or logical interface connects to an upstream switch or host. For example, the output line for ge-0/0/0 and ge-0/0/0.0 shows that the physical interface and the logical unit are both up and that an IPv4 address is present. This is a read-only confirmation you can make in seconds. A common usage pattern is to run show interfaces terse, find the candidate interface, then copy that name into a more detailed command such as show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive. A typical misconception is to assume the presence of an IP address implies traffic flows; it only indicates configuration and current assignment. To verify traffic, check the counters in the extensive output. Practically, start with terse for discovery, then expand only the interface you need to inspect in depth. show interfaces terse — find an interface quickly means show interfaces terse is the fastest way to locate interfaces and view basic up/down and protocol bindings.. In practical terms, using terse output to identify interfaces and addresses. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use terse for discovery
keyIdea.text: show interfaces terse is the fastest way to locate interfaces and view basic up/down and protocol bindings.

content.html:
Core Concept

show interfaces terse

Quickly lists interface names, admin/link states, and protocol bindings. Ideal for locating a port to inspect further.

Typical workflow
  1. Run show interfaces terse to locate the relevant interface name.
  2. Run the extensive command on that interface to view counters.
  3. Form a hypothesis (physical, routing, or resource) and test further.
Key Takeaway

Start with terse to identify candidates; it’s fast and non-disruptive.

Example output
# show interfaces terse
Interface               Admin Link Proto    Local                 Remote
ge-0/0/0                up    up
ge-0/0/0.0              up    up   inet     192.168.1.1/24
                                   inet6    fe80::.../64
Misconception
An interface showing up and an IP assigned does not guarantee good traffic; counters may reveal drops or CRC errors.
Check
If you see the interface here, run show interfaces <name> extensive next to read counters and errors.

screens.title: show interfaces <interface> extensive — read counters and status
screens.subtitle: Interpret speed, duplex, input/output errors, and drops

narration.text: The extensive interface output is where you diagnose traffic and link problems. It reports the link-level type, MTU, speed, duplex, administrative and physical state, and — critically — counters such as input errors, output errors, and drops. When you run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive, look for lines saying Physical link is Up and State: Up as basic health indicators. Then inspect Input errors and Output errors. For instance, rising CRC errors commonly indicate a physical-layer problem like a faulty cable or duplex mismatch. Drops, on the other hand, may indicate congestion or configuration issues such as policers or shaping. A common mistake is to focus only on speed and administrative state while ignoring error counters; those counters are often the primary clue for intermittent connectivity issues. A concrete example: if Input errors are non-zero and increasing, test with a known-good cable and check duplex settings on both ends. Finish by recording the counters and their direction of change to determine whether the issue is ongoing or historical. show interfaces <interface> extensive — read counters and status means non-zero and increasing error counters often point to physical or data link problems; use them to guide hardware checks or configuration corrections.. In practical terms, interpret speed, duplex, input/output errors, and drops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Error counters are clues
keyIdea.text: Non-zero and increasing error counters often point to physical or data link problems; use them to guide hardware checks or configuration corrections.

content.html:
Process Flow

From terse to extensive

After identifying an interface with terse, run the extensive view to inspect counters and physical parameters that reveal underlying problems.

Inspect these fields
  • Link-level type, MTU, Speed, Duplex — basic capability and negotiation.
  • State and Physical link is Up — confirm both administrative and physical link.
  • Input errors / Output errors / Drops — counters that indicate corruption, mismatch, or congestion.
Key Takeaway

Compare counters over time. Increasing error counts are actionable signals to check cables, interfaces, or duplex settings.

Example extensive output
# show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive
  Physical interface: ge-0/0/0, Enabled, Physical link is Up
  Link-level type: Ethernet, MTU: 1514, Speed: 1Gbps, Duplex: Full
  Input errors: 0, Output errors: 0, Drops: 0
Misconception
A stable 'Up' state alone does not guarantee error-free forwarding. Always check counters for CRC and drops.
Practical step
If you see CRC errors, swap the cable and verify duplex on both ends before replacing hardware.

screens.title: show route — inspect learned routes and next-hops
screens.subtitle: How to read the routing table and confirm route sources

narration.text: The routing table is the authoritative record of what the device will use to forward packets. show route lists learned routes, the protocol that supplied them, their preference, and next-hop information. When troubleshooting reachability, first query the table with either a full listing or a specific prefix, like show route 192.168.1.0/24. The output will indicate whether the route is active and show an arrow pointing to the next hop and interface. A common error is to assume that a routing protocol is operating purely because it’s configured; the routing table proves whether it is actually producing routes. For example, a default route 0.0.0.0/0 shown as *[OSPF/10] with a next hop via 192.168.1.2 indicates OSPF provided the route and which neighbor to reach. If a route is missing or the next hop is unexpected, you may have neighbor or redistribution issues. Use protocol-specific filters, such as show route protocol ospf or show route table inet.0, to narrow your focus and confirm the route's origin and status. show route — inspect learned routes and next-hops means always confirm route presence and next-hop in the routing table; configuration alone does not guarantee learned routes.. In practical terms, how to read the routing table and confirm route sources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Routing table is authoritative
keyIdea.text: Always confirm route presence and next-hop in the routing table; configuration alone does not guarantee learned routes.

content.html:
Comparison

How to read show route

Look for the destination prefix, the protocol tag and preference, and the active next-hop line that shows where packets will be sent.

Common filters
  • show route <prefix> — query a specific destination.
  • show route protocol ospf — view routes learned by OSPF only.
  • show route table inet.0 — view the default IPv4 unicast table.
Key Takeaway

Treat the routing table as your source of truth for reachability; use filters to focus on protocol or table of interest.

Example
# show route
inet.0: 10 destinations, 10 routes (10 active, 0 holddown, 0 hidden)
0.0.0.0/0          *[OSPF/10] 00:01:23, metric 1
                    > to 192.168.1.2 via ge-0/0/0.0
192.168.1.0/24     *[Direct/0] 00:02:45
                    > via ge-0/0/0.0
Misconception
Seeing a protocol configured does not mean routes exist. Always check the routing table for active routes and next-hops.
Pro tip
Use specific prefix queries to speed verification: show route 10.0.0.0/8 will tell you immediately if that destination is present.

screens.title: Filtering and routing table scopes
screens.subtitle: Targeting specific protocols and tables (inet.0) for focused troubleshooting

narration.text: Large routing tables can obscure the route you need. Junos supports filters so you can focus on a protocol or routing instance. For IPv4 unicast the primary table is inet.0. If you suspect OSPF is responsible for a route, run show route protocol ospf to display routes learned from OSPF only. This reduces noise and helps you spot missing routes, incorrect preferences, or unexpected next hops. Another practical pattern is querying a single prefix: show route 192.168.1.0/24 will immediately reveal whether the route is present, its active flag, and the next-hop. Common pitfalls include forgetting to check the correct routing instance when using virtual routing or VRFs, and assuming table names from other vendors—use inet.0 for default IPv4 unicast. When a route is present but points to an unexpected next-hop, investigate neighbor adjacencies, redistribution, or route-preference settings. Filtering narrows the scope of your diagnosis and helps you identify whether the control plane or external peers are the source of a problem. Filtering and routing table scopes means use protocol filters and table names to reduce noise and quickly find the routes that matter to your problem.. In practical terms, targeting specific protocols and tables (inet.0) for focused troubleshooting. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Filter to focus
keyIdea.text: Use protocol filters and table names to reduce noise and quickly find the routes that matter to your problem.

content.html:
Process Flow

Narrow your view

Apply filters so routing outputs show only what is relevant to your current question: protocol, table, or prefix.

Useful commands
  • show route table inet.0 — view the default IPv4 unicast table.
  • show route protocol ospf — show only OSPF-learned routes.
  • show route <prefix> — inspect a single destination quickly.
Key Takeaway

Filtering is a practical habit that saves time and points you directly at the protocol or table causing the issue.

Scenario
You expect a route from OSPF but cannot reach a subnet. Instead of scanning all routes, run:
show route protocol ospf
show route 10.0.0.0/8
show route table inet.0
Pitfall
Checking the wrong routing instance will show no routes. Ensure you query the correct table when using VRFs or non-default instances.
Practice tip
Start broad if unsure, then narrow with protocol or prefix-based filters as you gather evidence.

screens.title: Monitoring system health: processes, memory, storage, uptime
screens.subtitle: Commands to detect resource pressure and storage problems

narration.text: Beyond interfaces and routes, the device itself can be the root cause of issues. Use show system processes extensive to view C P U usage by process and to spot a runaway process that degrades forwarding. show system memory reports current R A M usage and available memory; low available memory can lead to instability or degraded control-plane functions. show system storage displays disk utilization — a full partition can prevent logging, backups, and even upgrades. Finally, show system uptime provides context about recent reboots that may explain transient states. A concrete example: if logging stops and a recent upgrade failed, check show system storage to see if the log partition is full. A common misconception is to assume C P U spikes always mean traffic problems; sometimes a management task or a faulty process consumes C P U. Use these commands to decide whether to reboot, clear logs, or troubleshoot the offending process. Regularly checking these metrics reduces the chance of surprise outages and streamlines maintenance planning. Monitoring system health: processes, memory, storage, uptime means cpu, memory, and storage checks help you detect resource issues that look like network problems but are actually system-level failures.. In practical terms, commands to detect resource pressure and storage problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: System metrics matter
keyIdea.text: CPU, memory, and storage checks help you detect resource issues that look like network problems but are actually system-level failures.

content.html:
Definition

System health commands

Inspect processes, memory, storage, and uptime to determine whether the system is contributing to network issues.

show system processes extensive
Shows CPU usage per process and helps identify runaway tasks.
show system memory
Reports memory allocation and free memory that supports control and data plane functions.
show system storage
Displays disk space; full storage can block logs and backups.
Key Takeaway

Include system health checks in routine monitoring to detect resource-driven incidents quickly.

Example commands and outputs
show system uptime
show system processes | no-more
show system memory
show system storage
Scenario
If user reports are intermittent, check processes and memory to rule out resource spikes before examining network-level causes.
Misconception
High CPU does not always mean heavy traffic; it can be a management or control-plane issue. Use precise process-level outputs to decide the next steps.

screens.title: Activity: Interface and Route Verification
screens.subtitle: Follow the verification steps used in a lab or production check

narration.text: This activity synthesizes the previous lessons into a routine check you can run after deployment or when diagnosing problems. First, log in to the device and run show interfaces terse to find the interface connected to the upstream switch; identify a name like ge-0/0/0. Second, run show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive and note Link-level type, MTU, Speed, State, and the Input and Output error counters. If you see non-zero errors, consider physical checks such as cable replacement or duplex negotiation. Third, run show route and look for a default route 0.0.0.0/0; if present, identify the next hop and protocol. Fourth, check system state with show system uptime and show system processes | no-more to inspect C P U-hungry processes. Each command builds evidence: interface state narrows to link issues, route presence confirms reachability, and system metrics rule out resource faults. A common pitfall is stopping after one command; continue through the steps to avoid misattributing the root cause. After finishing, record the key lines: interface state, error counters, default route and next hop, and C P U/memory highlights. In practical terms, follow the verification steps used in a lab or production check. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Repeatable checklist
keyIdea.text: A short, consistent verification checklist reduces diagnostic time and helps you collect the evidence needed to act correctly.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Interface and Route Verification

Follow these steps in your lab or on a device to verify interface health and route presence.

  1. Log in and run show interfaces terse to locate candidate interface name such as ge-0/0/0.
  2. Run show interfaces <interface> extensive and note Link-level, Speed, State, and error counters.
  3. Run show route and search for 0.0.0.0/0 to confirm default route and the next-hop address.
  4. Run show system uptime and show system processes | no-more to check for recent reboots and CPU-intensive processes.
Key Takeaway

Document observed counters and next hops. That record helps confirm whether an issue is transient or persistent.

Expected snippets
# show interfaces terse
ge-0/0/0                up    up
# show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive
  Physical link is Up
  Input errors: 0, Output errors: 0
# show route
0.0.0.0/0          *[OSPF/10]
  > to 192.168.1.2 via ge-0/0/0.0
If error counters are increasing, focus on physical checks and duplex settings. If the default route is missing, check neighbor adjacency and routing protocol state.

screens.title: Interpreting CRC and input error patterns
screens.subtitle: Common causes and the right next steps

narration.text: CRC and other input error increases are classic signals of physical issues. CRC errors occur when a frame's checksum doesn't match, indicating corrupted data on the wire. Typical causes include a damaged cable, bad transceiver, electromagnetic interference, or a duplex mismatch. When you see sustained CRC or input errors in show interfaces extensive, avoid immediately replacing unrelated hardware. First, verify duplex and speed negotiation on both ends of the link and try a known-good cable and a different port if available. If errors persist only on one interface, suspect the transceiver or the remote device. A frequent misconception is to blame routing or higher-layer protocols for CRC errors — those are data link layer issues. Another pattern is intermittent increases that correspond with heavy traffic; in that case, monitor drops and counters over time and correlate with traffic patterns. The correct discipline is to reproduce or observe the error trend, run simple physical tests, then escalate to replacing components if physical tests fail to clear the errors. Interpreting CRC and input error patterns means treat rising crc or input errors as physical-layer candidates; verify cabling and duplex before changing network configuration.. In practical terms, common causes and the right next steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Physical first
keyIdea.text: Treat rising CRC or input errors as physical-layer candidates; verify cabling and duplex before changing network configuration.

content.html:
Common Mistake

CRC and Input Errors

CRC and input error increases usually mean corrupted frames on the link. They are not routing problems and should be handled as physical or link-layer issues first.

Immediate checks
  • Verify duplex and speed on both ends of the link.
  • Replace the cable with a known-good cable and test again.
  • Swap the transceiver or try a different port if available.
Alert

Do not assume CRC errors are software or routing faults. Physical checks are the right first step.

Example diagnostics
# show interfaces ge-0/0/1 extensive
  Input errors: 345 CRC errors
  Output errors: 0
  Drops: 12

Next steps: check cable, verify duplex, swap transceiver
If swapping cable clears errors, you’ve found the cause. If errors persist across multiple ports and cables, the remote device or NIC may be faulty.

narration.text: Remember these core concepts as you monitor Junos devices. Operational mode is the safe, read-only context for show commands and should be your first stop during troubleshooting. The show interfaces command family gives both terse discovery and extensive counters; use terse to find interfaces and extensive to read error counters and physical parameters. The show route command shows the routing table and is the authoritative source for what the device will use to forward traffic; filter by protocol or prefix to focus your investigation. Finally, system health commands such as show system processes, show system memory, and show system storage reveal resource conditions that can mimic or cause networking problems. Keep these ideas in mind: collect evidence, form a hypothesis (physical, routing, or system), and then act. That disciplined approach reduces unnecessary changes and leads to faster resolution.

keyIdea.title: Memory snapshot
keyIdea.text: Operational checks + filters + system metrics = focused, low-risk troubleshooting.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for everyday use

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders at hand when monitoring a Junos device. First, start in operational mode and run show interfaces terse to find interfaces, then inspect counters with the extensive view. Second, verify routing decisions in show route; confirm the route exists, is active, and shows the expected next-hop and protocol. Third, include system health checks such as show system processes, show system memory, and show system storage to detect resource issues that can mimic networking faults. A short habit loop—observe, hypothesize, test—will help you avoid common mistakes like assuming a configured protocol equals a learned route or attributing data link errors to routing. Use filters and focused queries to speed diagnosis and reduce noise. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means observe (show commands), hypothesize (physical vs routing vs system), test (repeatable checks and filters).. In practical terms, three compact reminders for everyday use. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Key Concepts
Interfaces
Terse for discovery; extensive for counters and error diagnosis.
Routing
show route is the source of truth for forward paths and next-hops.
System Health
Check processes, memory, and storage to rule out system-induced failures.
Final Note

A short checklist—interfaces, routes, system—will make troubleshooting faster and more accurate.

ai_generation_note:
Create a 12-minute interactive video tutorial. Begin by logging into a Junos vSRX virtual machine. Demonstrate `show interfaces terse`, then `show interfaces ge-0/0/0 extensive`, highlighting the `State`, `Speed`, `Input errors`, and `Output errors` sections. Next, show `show route` and `show route 0.0.0.0/0`, explaining how to identify the active default route and its next-hop. Conclude by demonstrating `show system processes | no-more` and `show system uptime`. Use clear terminal output, with key information highlighted or zoomed in. Include a short interactive quiz question after the `show interfaces` demonstration asking to identify an issue based on error counters. Ensure captions and a transcript are available.
